title: Every Solo Agent Builder Eventually Reinvents a Worse Version of CI/CD - Sumaiya Shrabony
talk_summary: A solo builder of a 19-skill agent content pipeline describes how she unknowingly rebuilt CI/CD controls (regression tests, monitoring, contract tests, staging, audit trails) badly, and demos three 'polished but wrong' failures—voice drift, unverified claims, near-duplicate hooks—that pass a naive 'looks complete' check. Her fix is a small set of hard gates at the most expensive handoffs that block artifacts rather than warn, plus an audit record of which gate failed and why.

takeaways.technique: Hard blocking gates, not warning-only checks
takeaways.what_they_do: Each gate is a contract that stops the artifact from advancing to the next stage (e.g. publish-ready folder) when violated; warnings-only gates are explicitly rejected as 'suggestions'.
takeaways.evidence_quote: A gate which logs only warnings is not a gate. It's a suggestion. The gate needs to block the artifact from moving forward.

takeaways.what_they_do: Validates output schema/shape at each boundary between skills so a schema change in one skill doesn't silently break three downstream skills.
takeaways.evidence_quote: One skill changes its output schema, so three skills downstream break. You decided to add a validation at the boundary because of it.

takeaways.what_they_do: Any output containing factual claims must carry a verification log tracing each claim to a source; empty log blocks shipping.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Claim bearing content cannot ship without a verification trail. "Trust me" is not a verifier.

takeaways.technique: Map handoffs, gate the most expensive one first
takeaways.what_they_do: Enumerates every arrow between pipeline steps as a corruption point, then places the first gate where bad data costs the most, not where it's most complex.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Pick the most expensive handoff. Not the most complex, most expensive. The one where bad data can cost you the most.

takeaways.what_they_do: Every gate writes an audit record naming which gate failed, which contract was violated, and why, so a 2am scheduled failure is reconstructable from logs rather than the final artifact.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You need to know which gate failed. Which contract was violated and why? That's the audit trail.

takeaways.what_they_do: Compares new output's opening angle/hook against vault history and blocks near-duplicates even when each piece is individually coherent.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The hook, the opening angle, is a near duplicate of something from your vault history.
